sections.heading: Claims
sections.text: Session-scoped, single-request access control evaluates each call in isolation against a policy fixed for the session, which cannot express or catch composition — two individually-permitted actions ("read a confidential document," "send an external email") combined into an unauthorized disclosure. The paper's proposed fix, the **Agentic Principal Chain (APC)**, carries four pieces of state through a delegation hierarchy — authorization scope (resources, action types, data classifications, explicitly prohibited combinations), a chain of principals with per-hop delegation budgets, prior-action state, and pre-declared task intent — and admits a request only if it passes six conditions at once: identity binding to a verifiable chain position (C1), scope-plus-composition (in scope, not forming a prohibited pair/tuple with prior actions, within budget) (C2), context binding to the specific task instance and policy version (C3), single-use hash-bound approval tokens for high-impact actions (C4), evidence-sink reachability (C5), and consistency with the pre-declared intent (C6).

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Three separate evaluation methods against three existing adversarial benchmarks plus a self-designed adaptive suite: (1) deterministic composition-closure checking on InjecAgent (1,054 cases: 544 data-stealing, 510 direct-harm) and Agent Security Bench (400 attack tools across 10 scenarios) — does the admissibility predicate block the attacker's tool given session history; (2) a compromised-model simulation on AgentDojo (949 task-injection pairs across Workspace/Banking/Travel/Slack) that injects ground-truth attack tool calls directly into the pipeline after the first legitimate action, modeling full model compromise rather than prompt-injection specifically; (3) live utility measurement with Claude Sonnet 4.6 across the same AgentDojo domains to quantify the cost of enforcement on legitimate task completion. Two formal properties — Composition Soundness (no admissible action sequence produces a prohibited outcome given a complete restriction set) and Blast Radius Monotonicity (reachable authority is non-increasing at each delegation hop) — are stated and proved, not just tested. 99 multi-hop delegation-chain scenarios (depth 2–8) and 23 named adaptive attacks (43 variants, one set per authorization condition) round out the adversarial coverage.

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text:
- Exfiltration attack success rate on AgentDojo: 75–100% baseline → 0% under APC. Data-stealing ASR on InjecAgent: 100% → 0%. Disruptive-attack ASR on ASB: 100% → 0%. Destruction ASR (AgentDojo): 38.6% → 4.0%. Manipulation ASR (AgentDojo): 90.5% → 12.1%.
- Utility cost: −13.9 percentage points under strict enforcement, −8.6pp with a simulated human-approval interactive mode. Latency: 0.05ms median / 0.24ms p99 for a full six-condition check on an idle host (rising to 0.083–0.091ms p50 / 0.345–0.427ms p99 under contending load).
- **Authors' own stated limits, in full:** the action-class taxonomy "involves expert judgment; different security teams may derive different restriction sets"; the compromised-model evaluation "injects ground-truth attacks after the first legitimate step — a specific simulation methodology, not a universal worst case" and does not model an adversary interleaving legitimate and malicious calls across many turns; the 23 adaptive attacks "are self-designed rather than externally red-teamed"; "all benchmarks are synthetic, and no production-deployment data is presented"; residual risk concentrates in single-action misuse fully inside authorized scope (60.4% ASR on InjecAgent direct-harm — APC cannot catch a single call that is itself the harm), parameter-level attacks, coarse-grained intent-overlap (12 of 18 residual AgentDojo failures), an incomplete composition-restriction set (removing one prohibited pair raises data-stealing ASR to 39.9%), and attacks spanning multiple sessions, which need durable cross-session state APC does not provide; the two formal theorems are "not machine-checked; mechanized proofs are future work."
- The paper does **not** address concurrency: it does not propose or evaluate a bound on the number of simultaneously active sub-agents, and Theorem 4.8 explicitly assumes admission is serialized — "concurrent sub-agents require the PEP to serialize composition checks so TOCTOU violations do not arise" — a precondition, no
